cefrAlignment: After the fixes, each block matches its tag against the English Grammar/Vocabulary Profile and the British Council–EAQUALS Core Inventory. B1 items: present perfect with since, lend/borrow, first conditional, delayed, a simple booking dialogue and a notice. B2 items: past modal deduction, put off, non-defining which, would rather + past, and paraphrased detail in an announcement, a short article and a dialogue. C1 items: outweigh, not only inversion, it-cleft with not until … that, compelling, writer's implied attitude, a lecturer's main point against a misconception, and evaluating evidence. Difficulty rises in blocks p1–6, p7–13 and p14–20.
examFidelity: This is not an exam simulation. It is a 20-item, four-option placement screen with 6 B1, 7 B2 and 7 C1 items across grammar (7), vocabulary (5), reading (4) and listening (4). Each item now has exactly one defensible answer, and all 4 listening items can be answered from the spoken audio alone.
fixes: p7 (B2): replaced the past perfect item ('By the time we got to the cinema, the film had already started'). Past perfect is B1 in the English Grammar Profile and the Core Inventory. The new item tests past modal deduction ('The streets are all wet. It must have rained last night'), which is B2.

p11: the passage described a 'two-year study of a large travel company' where remote staff did 'slightly more' work. The well-known study of this kind (Ctrip; Bloom et al.) ran for nine months and found a 13% performance gain, so the text now says 'a study at one large company … completed more work'. Key unchanged.
p12: replaced the distractor 'not use' with 'not to use'. 'I'd rather you not use my phone' is standard American English, so the item had two defensible answers.
p13: Tom now says 'Anna, …' in the audio. TTS does not speak the speaker labels, so the stem's 'Anna' could not be identified by ear.

p17 (C1): replaced the what-cleft agreement item ('What I find most surprising is …'). What-clefts appear at B1/B2 in the English Grammar Profile. The new item is an it-cleft, 'It was not until she moved abroad that she realised …' (C1), and its distractor 'when' is a common learner error.

p19: softened historical claims that could not be verified ('For at least a century after Gutenberg, most printed books were religious or legal texts' became 'For decades … many … often in Latin'). Rebalanced option lengths, because the key was about 20 characters longer than any distractor. One distractor now tests careful listening ('mattered less than … schools and cheaper paper', whereas the talk says 'just as much').
openConcerns: recommendLevel thresholds are not edited (component out of scope). Current rule: C1 if B1 ≥ 0.7, B2 ≥ 0.7 and C1 ≥ 0.55; B2 if B1 ≥ 0.7 and B2 ≥ 0.5; otherwise B1. The design is sensible: it requires mastery of the lower levels plus at least 4/7 at the target level, and guessing alone never reaches B2. There are three problems. (1) With only 6 B1 items, the 0.7 gate allows a single error, which creates a cliff. For example, 4/6 B1 with 7/7 B2 and 7/7 C1 gives 'B1'. In a simple binomial model, about 18% of real B2 learners and 4% of C1 learners land on B1, mostly because of this gate. (2) There is no below-B1 outcome, so 0/20 is told 'B1 Intermediate'. (3) If speech synthesis is unavailable, the 4 listening items are scored wrong. Also, 0.5 and 0.55 both mean 4/7 in practice.

Suggested change for recommendLevel: C1 if C1 ≥ 4/7, B2 ≥ 5/7 and B1+B2 ≥ 10/13. B2 if (B1 ≥ 5/6 and B2 ≥ 4/7) or (B1 ≥ 4/6 and B2 ≥ 5/7). Otherwise B1, with a note that B1 lessons may be challenging when B1 ≤ 2/6. Leave listening items out of the denominators when TTS is unsupported. In the same model this cuts B2→B1 under-placement from about 18% to 10% and C1→B1 from about 4% to 0%, while B1→B2 over-placement rises slightly (24% → 28%).

The level tags are expert judgments and have not been calibrated. Pilot with learners of known level to confirm that item facility falls from B1 to C1 and that each item discriminates. p9, p10 and p11 sit at the B1+/B2 boundary (non-defining 'which' first appears at B1 in the EGP; p9 and p11 are explicit-detail questions), and p14 'outweigh' is a very frequent collocation that may behave like B2.
Twenty items give a large measurement error. The UI already says to treat the result as a starting point, which is appropriate.
learnerOutcome: A learner gets a quick, defensible estimate of whether to start with B1, B2 or C1 lessons, plus a per-area breakdown (grammar, vocabulary, reading, listening) that points to their weakest skill.
